w: What's tested The goal of denture occlusion: keep a prosthesis that floats on soft tissue in the mouth, so balance means resisting tipping Support, stability and retention: what each resists, and why stability matters most How a denture stays in: the film of saliva and the border seal more than suction, good fit, and above all muscle control; what resists tipping Resorption patterns (maxilla up and in, mandible down and out), skeletal Class I, II, III and pseudo-Class III, setting teeth over the ridge Balanced vs non-balanced (neutrocentric) vs lingualized occlusion: contacts in centric and eccentric positions, anterior contact, teeth and articulator settings, who gets which, and the slides' table comparing them Centric occlusion, not MIP, in a denture; Hanau's Realeff: build and check the occlusion on an articulator; Thielemann's formula and which factors are fixed Denture teeth: porcelain, composite and acrylic; anatomic (30-33°), semi-anatomic (12-22°) and flat (0°) tooth forms; how the teeth are chosen On 11/5 Dr. Givan took "a different turn": occlusion on dentures. He is required to present it before the class has had its denture course (that starts in January, with him), so he stepped back to explain what a denture is and how it works. The whole goal is different from the dentate patient: with removable occlusion the goal is to keep the prosthesis in the mouth and have some kind of function. A complete denture is fabricated from fairly sophisticated plastics and essentially floats on the tissues: no connection, no attachment. Patients who call them "my upper plate and my lower plate" aren't wrong: picture a plate from your cabinet trying to stay in position in someone's mouth. If occlusion is bringing the jaws together, how the dentures fit together decides whether they stay in. Denture words Denture teeth are not teeth: no pulp, no enamel or dentin, no biology, just a tooth-colored piece of plastic that mimics a tooth. They are attached to a plastic denture base, the part that fits over the tissues; how well the base is adapted to the tissues plays a large role in how well the denture stays in. The extensions that come up into the vestibule on each side are the denture flange, and the extent of the flange, as far as it can go before reaching the boundary between moving and non-moving tissues, is the peripheral border. A patient with no teeth is edentulous; fully edentulous means none remain. Their dentures are complete dentures or full dentures, as opposed to partial dentures, when some teeth are present. The terms aren't great, he admits, but they are what we have. When teeth are lost, the bone goes away: resorption. Patients who have lost a lot of it find it very hard to eat and keep up their nutrition, particularly with the lower jaw. That problem, edentulism, is what drove the development of dental implants almost 50 years ago: "we must have dental implants in order to be able to retain a denture." It wasn't the single-tooth implant or the fixed hybrid that drove it. A short history: what role did occlusion play? "What do I really want you to know from this is essentially... what was the role of occlusion in this? And you're going to find out the answer will be practically none." The history slides are all marked "No test questions": know the point, not the names and dates. The earliest dentures were carved, from wood and later ivory, before impressions or models existed, and they were made mostly for esthetics: people felt they looked better with teeth. A few have knobs at the back that suggest an attempt at chewing surfaces, but there was no real occlusion. In the 1600s and 1700s, carved ivory prostheses had hinges or springs at the back for opening and closing (ivory breaks down in the mouth too). You couldn't really speak or eat with them; they were for those who could afford them. Pierre Fauchard, the father of dentistry, published a design for a carved ivory denture with flexible metal springs: again, not functional. By the late 1600s impressions could be taken in beeswax and poured in plaster of Paris, so pieces could be made to come on and off. George Washington's teeth were not wooden. His dentist, John Greenwood, made several sets, carved from ox bone and ivory, many with a swaged gold base and springs at the back. Both George and Martha Washington had the same complaints denture wearers have today: their letters to Greenwood, in the Reynolds Historical Library at UAB, say it hurts here on the side and is uncomfortable to eat and talk. Washington was a man of few words, and it isn't surprising why. Dentures came to fit well enough to use a little suction: James Gardette found that a well-fitting base is held by atmospheric pressure. It is still one way we keep a maxillary denture in (occasionally a mandibular one), though the first sip of a hot liquid breaks it. Human teeth taken from corpses were used for a time ("not our most ethical day in dentistry"), and bases were made of materials such as cellulose that didn't hold up. Then came porcelain: Duchâteau's porcelain dentures (about 1774) chipped and looked too white, and in 1808 Fonzi made individually fired porcelain teeth, his "terro-metallic incorruptible" teeth, that could stay in the mouth without breaking down. Claudius Ash's teeth became popular, with occlusal holes, dots and ridges that didn't mimic human anatomy. Bonwill made the first real attempt at denture occlusion: he designed teeth to meet a function, arranging arbitrarily formed molds so they kept contact in motion, and set them to his equilateral triangle, the origin of the occlusal plane, with the idea that if the teeth stayed touching all the time, the denture would stay in the mouth. No springs or wires from upper to lower. That is why he is known as the father of articulation. Bases improved too: vulcanite, rubber cross-linked with sulfur, was hugely popular (and dental labs, smelling of sulfur, were something you didn't want to live next to), and tooth and lab industries grew. Ideas about what the teeth should look like weren't well understood. The temperamental theory, going back to antiquity, held that denture teeth should follow the patient's personality or temperament; it was widely accepted and poorly understood, and it is still with us: denture molds are still described as bold or soft. J. Leon Williams' geometric forms said to shape the teeth like the patient's face: ovoid, square or tapered, also still used today. By the early 20th century more science was applied: Alfred Gysi, working with the Dentists' Supply Company (later Dentsply), perfected balanced occlusion, designing teeth that follow the motion of the mandible to keep the teeth together in bilateral balance, and was the first to use a central bearing device. His Trubyte teeth, from the 1910s, are still sold by Dentsply, among the best-selling denture teeth for over 125 years. So the history of denture occlusion has nothing to do with the things we talk about for the dentate mouth: where the forces go, posterior disclusion, anterior guidance. With a denture, the goal is to keep it from tipping out of the mouth. Balance refers to countering those tipping motions. Why denture occlusion is different We still want the edentulous patient to chew, speak and swallow. But years of developing neuromuscular function with the natural teeth are not on your side: the proprioception of the teeth and alveolar tissues is gone, and patients have only a vague sense of where they are. In many ways a patient with dentures has one upper tooth and one lower tooth: the denture teeth never operate independently; an upper prosthesis and a lower prosthesis work together. So the arrangement of the denture teeth is all about preventing tipping of the denture when the teeth are brought into contact. That is the whole goal of balancing: "balancing being contrasted as the opposite of tipping." If, in a right working movement, there is contact on both the right and the left side at the same time, the denture won't tip out, and it stays in better function. Those are balancing contacts, the very contacts we avoid in natural teeth. How a denture stays in the mouth Physical forces. The slides sort them. Contributing less: atmospheric pressure, vacuum, adhesion, cohesion and the seating force. Contributing more: the interposed fluid, the film of saliva between the base and the tissues (its flow, its viscosity and how thin the film is), and surface tension at the periphery. They depend on the patient's saliva (viscous or thin; it changes with age, and most denture patients are older) and on extension to the periphery: a good border seal keeps air from seeping under the denture and letting it drop or tip. All of them require good adaptation and a border seal. On a cone beam CT of a patient wearing a denture, dark spaces between the base and the tissues show misfit, and where there is misfit, suction and cohesion become almost impossible to capture. And most of them are undone in function, especially by hot liquids: even with good fit, they aren't strong enough to hold a denture while the patient chews. Muscle control. What really keeps a denture in is the musculature. Some patients develop neuromuscular control that keeps even the worst-fitting denture in place, and they eat fine; others can't manage the best denture you could make. "Muscle control is likely to be the most important factor to keep a denture in place." And remember: most of the time patients have their teeth apart, so adhesion, cohesion and muscle control are what hold the denture then. Two more points from the slides: undercuts in the ridge help only a little, and they can make the denture painful; and an ill-fitting denture makes resorption worse. What resists tipping, and what makes it harder Structures have to be in the way to keep a denture from moving, and as they are lost, it gets harder. The slides list what resists tipping. Anatomy: the ridge height, ridge width and ridge shape, the depth of the palatal vault ("a big one for the maxillary denture") and the type of posterior palatal seal. Denture design: the fit of the intaglio surface, the side that rests on the tissues, and occluding contacts that don't move the denture. You will assess the anatomy in the denture course. Some tissues are more compressible than others, particularly toward the soft palate. Because heat-processed resin shrinks, a posterior palatal seal is added at the back to push into the soft tissues and overcome the shrinkage; milled dentures fit intimately enough that it isn't always needed. "If you always remember this: all removable is movable." Every removable prosthesis has some motion, and we design it to resist that motion. The soft tissues under it vary in thickness and are resilient, so every time the teeth hit, the tissue sinks a little and the denture moves. That is why the occlusion often can't be developed in the mouth: it is built and adjusted outside the mouth, on an articulator. Hanau called this tissue effect the Realeff, short for "resiliency and like effect" (the slides also write "resilient and like effect"); it has been known in dentistry for over a century. Resorption follows patterns. The maxilla resorbs up and in, so its supporting arch gets smaller than the original arch; the mandible resorbs down and out, so at the level where the teeth are supposed to be, the edentulous mandible becomes larger than the dentate one. The slides give the direction for each region: Maxillary anterior Upward and toward the posterior (inward) Maxillary posterior Upward and toward the midline Mandibular anterior Downward and toward the anterior (forward) Mandibular posterior Downward and away from the midline (outward) Denture teeth are generally set near where the ridge is ("not rocket science"), so we often have to set them in crossbite, and that's fine: there's nothing wrong with a crossbite in a denture. The jaws also started out different sizes. A skeletal Class I (orthognathic) relationship has the jaws roughly matched in size and shape; in skeletal Class II (retrognathic) the mandible is smaller and set back; skeletal Class III (prognathic) is the opposite. These are related to Angle's molar classes. A patient who becomes a skeletal Class III because the mandible resorbs outward while the maxilla resorbs inward has a pseudo-Class III relationship. "What I want you to know today": the skeletal Class I, II and III relationships, and pseudo-Class III from resorption. All of this affects where the teeth go, which he will teach in January. Two more factors you can't get around. The tongue hypertrophies after the teeth are lost ("nature abhors a vacuum"): it fills the space where the teeth used to be, mostly a problem for the lower denture. And a recent extraction patient, with plenty of bone, is not easier: they are often harder, because a denture needs room for its base and teeth, and limited interarch space makes it much more difficult. Support, stability and retention The three most important things about any removable prosthesis. Asked on his specialty boards, he answered "without even firing up a neuron": support, stability and retention. "If there are three things I want you to remember off this slide." Support Vertical force toward the tissues (closing and compressing the dentures) Some areas take it well: the buccal shelf and retromolar pad below, the palate above (the primary support areas); the ridges themselves aren't good at it Retention Vertical dislodgement, away from the tissues What patients focus on: peanut butter holds the dentures together as the jaw opens, the tongue lifts the lower denture. It bothers them, but it doesn't hurt Stability Horizontal force (sideways movement) The most important: a denture that slides sideways when they bite is extraordinarily painful, and they can't eat "Of all the things that we need to address, stability is the most important." It is the one thing a dental implant is fabulous at: even two implants address stability, and that is life-changing for a patient who couldn't eat. Retention from implants is a plus. Humans are among the worst for stability: we don't chew like a shark, straight up and down; we move the jaw side to side. Denture occlusion, the shapes of the teeth as they fit together, contributes to all three, especially stability. The three are related: tipping is a horizontal movement, and it can also dislodge the denture, which is retention. How the occlusion helps support, from the slides: the contacts must be bilateral, equal and simultaneous, on a well-fitting prosthesis. In centric occlusion both schemes direct the force toward the ridges, onto the primary support areas: non-balanced through a flat plane parallel to the denture base, balanced through cusp-to-fossa contact. Centric relation and centric occlusion in a denture When the muscles of a denture patient contract, they seat the joints, so centric relation is pretty easy to find (most patients don't posture forward, though some skeletal Class IIs will). Contact of the denture teeth with the joints seated is centric occlusion: the joints seated and the denture teeth fully interdigitated, as best they're designed to. MIP is not a term used for dentures: maximum intercuspation is a neuromuscular response, and there is no neuromuscular response with a denture. In centric occlusion, the denture teeth contact usually only in the posterior. The anterior teeth are protected, because the bone at the front of the edentulous maxilla, the premaxilla, doesn't take forces well once the teeth are gone. All the occlusal function is generally on the posterior teeth; the anteriors are for appearance. The occlusal schemes To keep a denture stable there are two basic approaches, plus a middle ground: 1. Balanced occlusion. Bonwill's idea of 125 years ago: keep the denture teeth touching everywhere the patient moves, in centric occlusion and in every eccentric position. It is also called bilateral balance (almost redundant: if it isn't balanced on both sides it isn't balanced) or anatomic occlusion, a widely used term he dislikes, since there is nothing natural about it. 2. Non-balanced occlusion. Contact in centric occlusion, but the denture is designed so it can't contact anywhere else: flat teeth, a flat occlusal plane, and an articulator set to something completely unlike the patient. The condylar guidance is set to zero; the patient never has zero, so whatever condylar guidance they have separates the dentures as they move. There is no anterior contact. Not contacting is another way to keep a denture from tipping. The slides also call it neutrocentric occlusion. 3. Lingualized occlusion. A modification: a tooth with an elongated maxillary lingual cusp that fits against a flat plane or a wide fossa on the mandibular teeth, "a little bit like a mortar and pestle." It is hugely popular because it is much easier to arrange the teeth, it can be set balanced or non-balanced, and it is most likely the scheme you will use for many of your dentures. "That's why I like making these tables for you, because this table will basically give you the one how-to of how all this fits together": In centric occlusion Posterior teeth contact Posterior teeth contact Maxillary lingual cusps contact the mandibular teeth In eccentric positions Contact on both sides (working and non-working) and in protrusion No contact in any eccentric position Balanced: contact in eccentric movements too (left-right balance); non-balanced: none Anterior contact Allowed in protrusion with anatomic teeth (the posteriors stay in contact); with semi-anatomic teeth only if the plane or curve compensates None No: difficult, though it can be compensated (in class: never, since it can't be kept from tipping front to back) Posterior teeth Anatomic (30-33°) or semi-anatomic Flat (0°) Semi-anatomic maxillary teeth with a long lingual cusp, against 0-12° mandibular teeth with a wide fossa Articulator Programmed to match the patient: semi-adjustable, facebow, protrusive record Condylar guidance set to 0° As for the scheme chosen Plane and compensating curve Used to keep the teeth together Flat: no compensating curve Flat when non-balanced; a little plane and curve to balance Both balanced and non-balanced work well, and patients accept both. They differ in esthetics, in stability, and in whether anterior contact can be allowed: protrude a denture with the front teeth touching and it is very easy to tip and dislodge. Balanced occlusion By definition, balanced occlusion is the bilateral, simultaneous contact of the anterior and posterior teeth in centric and eccentric positions. In a working movement there is contact on both the left and the right side; if contact were on one side only, the one-piece upper or lower denture would be destabilized and might tip out, and patients can't work with that. Bilateral balance had been around a long time, but the person who made it easier was Rudolph Hanau, an engineer, not a dentist. He saw that you can't create the occlusion in the mouth, because the tissues keep moving: he named it the Realeff ("resiliency and like effect"). So the occlusion is built on an articulator. If you try to mark a denture occlusion in the mouth with articulating paper, the denture tips as it squeezes into the soft tissues, everything marks, and it gives you the wrong information; the denture course teaches the clinical remount instead. The slides add Hanau's own rules: his balanced occlusion used heavy contacts on the first molars to make up for the Realeff of the soft tissues and the joints, and the precise balance built on an articulator isn't present in the mouth, so it is refined through clinical remounts, never by adjusting the occlusion in the mouth. Hanau also gave us the relationships among the five determinants of occlusion (Hanau's quint). Thielemann's articulation formula (the one the Review lecture spells Thielmann) shows them as proportions: balance = (condylar guidance × anterior guidance) / (cusp angle × compensating curve × plane of occlusion). It first said incisal guidance; later, anterior guidance. Early on, cusp angle and cusp height were used interchangeably; today cusp angle is the term for dentures and cusp height for the natural dentition. The determinants were first used for their original purpose, keeping denture teeth together. For example, if you increase the plane of occlusion, then to keep the teeth together you flatten the compensating curve or use a flatter tooth. For the dentate patient we take the same principles and turn them around to keep the teeth apart: the same tool, used differently. The slides sort the factors. Fixed: the condylar guidance (the patient's joints; you cannot change it) and the plane of occlusion, aligned to the interpupillary line and Camper's (ala-tragus) plane, which affects esthetics. In class he said the plane can change only a little: there can't be a negative plane, where you see the posterior teeth before the anterior teeth ("an aesthetic crime"). Variable: the anterior guidance (possible with anatomic teeth steep enough, difficult with semi-anatomic teeth, and mostly unused, since the anterior teeth usually don't touch), the compensating curve and the cusp angle (the teeth chosen). So balance comes mainly from the compensating curve, the cusp angle and what little the plane of occlusion can change. A balanced setup on an articulator: the sagittal condylar inclination is set from a protrusive record, the plane of occlusion by Camper's line and the interpupillary line, and a compensating curve is built in. In centric occlusion the teeth intercuspate; in a working movement there are contacts on both sides, and on the non-working side at the same time. It is not easy to set up; that technique is January's, and much of it will be digital in your future. Non-balanced occlusion Defined: flat (zero-degree) teeth set in an anteroposterior plane parallel to the denture foundation (the ridges), with no guidance and no compensating curve. Drawn, it looks a bit ugly, but it works. The slides call it the neutrocentric concept (citing Sears, 1949, and DeVan, 1954): neutralize the inclines and centralize the forces. The thinking behind it: does bilateral balance even apply while chewing? With a bolus of food between the teeth, there is no balance at all, and the chance of tipping a denture is very significant. That is why denture patients are trained to put food on both sides of the mouth, chew as vertically as they can, avoid big bites (biting into a sandwich tips the back down and flips the lower denture up) and chew on the premolars rather than the incisors: "the incisors are for smiling, but the posterior teeth allow you to chew." Only as the food breaks down do the teeth come together. "Enter bolus, exit balance," as the slides quote it (from Prime, and from Boucher in 1961). So the non-balanced idea: allow contact only on closure into centric occlusion, separate in every eccentric movement, and keep the forces centralized, never lateral or horizontal. The neutralizing factors are the cusp angle, the plane of occlusion, the compensating curve and the anterior guidance, all made flat, and the articulator's condylar guidance is artificially set to zero. The slides give five tooth factors. Position: as far lingual as the tongue allows. Proportion: the buccolingual width narrowed by 40% to decrease the stress on the ridge. Pitch: parallel to the planes of the denture bases, with no compensating curve and no anterior guidance (the patient is told not to incise in protrusion). Form: cuspless. Number: the mandibular second molars may be removed to keep the occlusion flat ahead of the ascending ramus, which starts to rise there. That makes it very easy to set up. The old flat teeth weren't esthetic, but they functioned well even for patients without good ridge height. Today's flat teeth have functionally flat surfaces that don't look flat, and with most of the esthetics coming from the anterior teeth, they look fine. Lingualized occlusion The middle ground. The slides define it: semi-anatomic maxillary teeth with an elongated palatal (lingual) cusp, against 0-12° mandibular teeth with a widened fossa, and no contact of the buccal cusps: a mortar-and-pestle contact that helps grind the food. Its early form simply tipped a 12° tooth against a 0° tooth, which opened the buccal space too much; today's teeth are made for it and look better, with the interdental spaces closed. Non-balanced lingualized: contact in centric occlusion only; the lingual cusps hit and there is no eccentric contact. Balanced lingualized: contact in centric occlusion and in eccentric movements, the lingual cusp sitting in the fossa, with a little plane of occlusion and compensating curve to give left-right balance. Anterior contact: in class he said never, because it can't be kept from tipping front to back; the slides' table says no, it is difficult, though it can be compensated. It is widely used in the school's clinic. Which way to set it depends on what the patient brings. Non-balanced: a lot of ridge resorption, flabby tissues, poor oral awareness or dexterity, difficult jaw relations. Balanced: healthy, good ridges, firm mucosa, good awareness and good muscular dexterity. The slides list seven advantages: the centric contacts move half a tooth lingual, a more favorable lever; the force is centered over the ridge crest (slightly lingual in the molar area); there is only one contact point; minimal frictional contact; the maxillary buccal cusps are buccalized, leaving escape ways for food; working and balancing contacts are simpler, since only one cusp occludes; and it works with any ridge morphology, so with almost any patient, young to old. It is also easier to set. Disadvantage: with fewer teeth touching, wear shows sooner, and the patient may lose vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO). The four schemes compared The slides end the schemes with a summary table: subjective ratings, from − (a drawback) up to +++ (the strongest). Esthetics +++ + + − Penetration of food + + + − Stability during function ++ + − − Simpler technique − − + ++ Less precise records − − + ++ Decreased lateral forces − − + ++ Ease of adjustment − + ++ +++ Class II and III jaw relations − − + + Stability with centralized forces − − + + Read it as a trade: balanced wins on esthetics and on stability during function; the flatter and less balanced the scheme, the simpler it is to make, record and adjust, the less lateral force it puts on the ridges, and the better it suits Class II and III jaw relations. Denture teeth: what they're made of Esthetics Very esthetic, often the most Good; layers improve translucency Fair; may stain Wear Minimal, so it maintains the vertical dimension Multi-cross-linked for wear resistance, but it still wears: in 5-7 years the teeth are worn to a reverse curve and chew inefficiently Less wear resistance Bond to the denture base None: held mechanically, with pins (anterior teeth) or diatorics, holes with undercuts (posterior teeth) Chemical bond Chemical bond to the acrylic base Handling May chip or fracture; denser and harder than crown and bridge porcelain, so difficult to set and adjust; clicks against each other Don't chip; softer sounds; easier to adjust and polish; expensive Low cost; easy to shape and adjust; can be ground to fit a small interarch distance Used for High-end dentures The most common: most good dentures today, the number one go-to Mainly temporary (interim) prostheses Composite and cross-linked teeth come in many molds (one line on the slides offers up to 26 upper and 15 lower anterior molds and 8 posterior molds) and in shade systems such as Vita's: 16 shades in four groups, A to D, plus 2 bleach shades. When denture teeth wear, the patient closes farther, so wear can cost vertical dimension: you want the highest wear resistance you can get. Choosing the teeth Denture teeth come from manufacturers' mold charts (for example Dentsply's True Expression, or Ivoclar's BlueLine DCL, dual cross-linked, which the school uses most). The teeth are engineered in sets: a particular maxillary posterior tooth is meant to articulate with a particular mandibular posterior tooth, "just like a ball and socket." You choose one maxillary anterior mold clinically (his example: A22). The chart gives its measurements (canine to canine, measured flat or on the curve of the arch, and the length of the central incisor) and its shape, then lists what is engineered to go with it: the mandibular anterior mold (A3) and the posterior molds for each occlusal scheme. In Ivoclar's language: orthoplane (flat, 0°, non-balanced), ortholingual (lingualized, balanced or non-balanced), orthotyp (semi-anatomic) and postaris (anatomic, for full bilateral balance). "The first take-home point about denture occlusion is that the denture occlusion is entirely based upon whatever selection we make to pick out that anterior maxillary mold." Everything else is engineered to follow it. And the anterior mold is chosen more on esthetics than occlusion. Personality still shows up: every manufacturer's chart still has soft and bold molds (the temperamental theory, alive in 2026), and general shapes, square, tapering or ovoid (even combinations, "if you're the indecisive type"). Clinical guides: the wax rim on a record base, shaped in the mouth (January), shows the lip support, where the incisal edge goes (how far forward and how long the teeth should be), the midline and the canine positions, and its shape becomes the occlusal plane: the teeth are set to fit the wax rim. Berry's ratio (his biometric method, 1906): the central incisor about 1/16 of the bizygomatic width. "Do you think that's scientifically valid? And the answer is absolutely not. Does it tend to work for a lot of patients? ... Yeah, it actually does." The ala-to-ala width of the nose, with a gauge, suggests small, medium or large molds and correlates somewhat with canine position: not scientifically valid either, but a quick way to something that looks good. A recurring theme in tooth selection. The posterior tooth form depends on the scheme you build: non-balanced needs flat teeth. Factors in choosing: the patient's neuromuscular control, the arch (ridge) morphology, the jaw relations (Class I, II, III), the interarch distance ("a big one"), the arch length, and whether they have worn dentures before: even experienced wearers start from ground zero with new dentures. Also shade: natural, fitted to the patient's complexion; the brightest and whitest can look fake ("you don't want headlights"). Denture teeth tend to be smaller than natural teeth, because they are easier to set. Larger arches need larger molds. The slides give six criteria for the posterior teeth: the color, in harmony with the anterior teeth; a buccolingual width less than the natural teeth; an occlusogingival length set by the interarch distance and in harmony with the length of the canine; a mesiodistal length that fills the space from the distal of the canine to the retromolar pad; the cuspal inclination; and the material. Tooth forms compared Cusp angle 30-33° (the handout: 30° or more): sulci, ridges, look like teeth Lower, about 12-22° depending on the mold (the 12° and 20° molds); lingualized maxillary teeth belong here 0° Scheme Balanced; can let the anterior teeth touch in protrusion Balanced or not; lower lateral forces; can't support anterior contact unless the plane or curve compensates Non-balanced For it Best esthetics; chewing efficiency (controversial); resist rotation of the base; guide jaw closure into centric; less force per unit area on the ridges; the incisal guidance can be balanced Easier stability; can still be set in balance Least lateral force, so stability is easiest; any jaw relation (Class I, II, III) and crossbite; simpler to adjust; poor neuromuscular control; fewer complications Against it Needs a protrusive record and a facebow on a semi-adjustable articulator; more skill (a technician sets one in 20 minutes, your first takes days); hard to refine; more horizontal force through the cusps, so more bone deformation; short-lived results as the denture settles and inexpensive teeth wear; difficult with abnormal jaw relations Not quite as esthetic Less esthetic (old ones "dog-ugly"); poor penetration of food, so more pressure on the ridges and more lateral chewing; difficult to balance; a psychological drawback for some patients. Clinically acceptable Other names, from the slides: semi-anatomic teeth are also called functional or anatoline teeth; non-anatomic teeth are also called cuspless, zero-degree, rational, flat-plane or monoline teeth. Some claims have no support, he said: that cusps give the patient a "point of return" through neuromuscular feedback (there is none with a denture; the slides still list it among the advantages of cusps), or that a flat tooth is uncomfortable to close against. What the evidence says Balanced occlusion with good anatomic teeth gives the very best esthetics, but even today's non-balanced flat teeth look "pretty darn good," and esthetics has never held him back from a non-balanced occlusion when it was best for the patient. Anatomic teeth do penetrate and grind food better, but that isn't clinically significant: flat-plane, non-balanced dentures are clinically just as successful, and patients maintain great nutrition. "Both of them cross the finish line just fine." The ability to masticate is one factor of many in selecting teeth. Most patients simply want to smile at their grandchildren and eat a nice meal without embarrassment, and any of these schemes can get them there. The slides cite a systematic review (Abduo, 2013, in the International Journal of Prosthodontics): anatomic teeth set in balanced or lingualized occlusion are preferable to flat teeth set non-balanced, mainly for patient acceptance. The literature is inconclusive but tends to favor cusps, and all the schemes are generally successful. Looking ahead: partial dentures and implants Not everybody loses all their teeth. For a partial denture it's simple: the more teeth that have been lost, the more you think like a denture, an occlusion that keeps the prosthesis stable, with support, stability and retention. The more natural teeth remain, the more you think like the dentate patient: canine guidance or group function, and posterior disclusion, because the teeth are in charge, not the prosthesis. With implants, more factors come in: what the opposing arch is, how many implants were placed, and the reminder that every removable prosthesis has some motion, such as rotation. The mindset: denture occlusion is all about keeping the prosthesis in the mouth. The denture teeth are parts of an upper prosthesis and a lower prosthesis, each working as a single unit, so balance means resisting tipping, and stability is the property that matters most. Complete dentures start in January in the PCD course, with him.
